notes.meaning: Moses placed the fat portions of the ram and the bread into the hands of Aaron and his sons. Together they waved them back and forth before the Lord to present them as an offering. This act was called the filling of the hands, showing that God was filling their hands with holy work for His service.

Moses took the pieces back from their hands and burned them on the altar over the burnt offering. Consuming these portions completely in fire showed full devotion to the Lord. The rising smoke was a sweet-smelling gift that was pleasing to God.

Moses took the ram's breast and waved it before the Lord as a special offering. Because Moses was acting as the priest for this service, this portion was given to him to eat. It was his rightful reward for doing God's work during their ordination.

God set apart the breast that was waved and the thigh that was lifted up as the regular share for Aaron and his sons. The breast was moved back and forth and the thigh lifted up to show they belonged to God before the priests received them to eat. This rule taught the people that caring for their priests was part of their ongoing fellowship with God.

Aaron's holy garments were not thrown away when he died; they were preserved for his descendants. Future high priests would put on these same sacred robes when they were anointed and ordained. This reminded Israel that the high priest's office continued even as individual leaders passed away.

The son who succeeded Aaron as high priest had to wear the holy robes for seven days while ministering in the sanctuary. This week of preparation gave the new leader time to reflect quietly on the weight of his duties. It also ensured that a full Sabbath passed over him during his installation.

The remaining meat was boiled in a holy area, and the priests ate it with the bread at the entrance of the tent. Sharing this sacred meal showed friendship and peaceful fellowship between God and His newly ordained servants. No outsider was allowed to eat it because the food had been used for atonement—the ceremony that covered their sins and made them right with God.

Any meat or bread left over until the following morning had to be burned with fire. Because the food was set apart as holy, it could not be allowed to spoil or be eaten like an ordinary meal. This strict rule protected the dignity of God's sacred things.

Moses was told to repeat these ordination rites every day for seven full days. Consecration was not treated as a quick or casual event. Setting aside a full week gave Aaron and his sons time for calm, reverent reflection on their holy calling.

Each day a bull was offered as a sin offering to make atonement, which means paying the price to take away sin and restore peace with God. The altar was also wiped clean, anointed with holy oil, and set apart. Even though the altar itself could not sin, it needed cleansing because it was built and used by sinful human hands.

After seven days of cleansing, the altar became most holy. Anything placed upon the altar was claimed by God and set apart completely for His use. The altar was so holy that it made the gifts offered upon it acceptable to the Lord.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view this as an early ritual concept where physical contact with a most holy object was believed to pass on holiness automatically, bringing danger to anyone unauthorized who touched it.

notes.meaning: God commanded Israel to sacrifice two one-year-old lambs on the altar every single day. One lamb was offered in the morning and the other in the evening at twilight. This regular sacrifice reminded the nation each day of their need for God's mercy and invited them to renew their devotion morning and evening.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars propose that these verses were inserted later from Numbers 28, suggesting that in earlier times only the morning offering included a burnt animal sacrifice.

notes.meaning: Along with each lamb, the priest offered fine flour mixed with olive oil, as well as a drink offering of wine poured out before the Lord. The flour and oil represented the fruit of the people's daily work presented back to God. Together, the meat, bread, and wine formed a complete meal offered to God on behalf of the nation.

The evening lamb was offered with the same grain and drink offerings as the morning sacrifice. When burned on the altar, its smoke rose as a pleasant aroma that satisfied the Lord. This daily pattern closed the day just as it began, in total dedication to God.

This daily burnt offering was to continue for all generations at the entrance of the Tent of Meeting. That doorway was the place where the Lord promised to meet Moses and speak with him. God gave these laws not merely to set up rituals, but to maintain living communion with His people.

God promised that He would meet with the entire nation of Israel at the sanctuary. The tent was not made holy merely by its materials, but by the glorious presence of God Himself. When the Lord revealed His glory there, He set the whole assembly apart as His treasured people.

The Lord declared that He Himself would consecrate the tent, the altar, and Aaron and his sons. The ceremonies performed by Moses were outward signs, but only God could make anything truly holy. It was God's own grace that gave the priests their authority to serve in His presence.

The supreme goal of building the sanctuary and offering sacrifices was so that God could live among His people. He promised to make His dwelling in their midst and be their personal God. This special covenant promise shows God's desire to live in close fellowship with those who trust Him.

Through God's continual presence, the Israelites would truly understand that He was the Lord their God. He had delivered them from slavery in Egypt for this great purpose: so that He might dwell among them. His mighty acts of rescue were done to bring them into a lasting relationship with Himself.
